title: Transition-metal colour & complexes
examples: Why are some metal compounds coloured?
What causes the colour change in metal ions?
How does the type of ligand affect the colour?

explain.say: Today we will look at why some metal compounds show colour.
When ligands approach the metal ion, they cause the d-orbitals to split.
The energy difference between these split levels is called the crystal field splitting energy.
The colour observed depends on the energy gap between the split d-orbitals.
A common example is the complex ion $ ext{Cu}^{2+}$ which absorbs light in the red region.
In everyday life, the colour of stained glass windows is due to metal ions.

faq.q: Why is the colour of a complex ion dependent on the ligands?
faq.a: The ligands change the strength of the interaction with the metal ion. This changes the size of the energy gap, which dictates the colour absorbed.
asks: Does the ligand determine the colour?
How do ligands affect the energy gap?

faq.q: What happens to the d-orbitals when they split?
faq.a: The five degenerate d-orbitals split into different energy levels. The energy difference between these levels is key to understanding the colour.

faq.q: If the energy gap is large, what colour will the complex be?
faq.a: A large energy gap means the complex absorbs high-energy light, which corresponds to the blue or violet end of the visible spectrum.
asks: High energy gap means what colour?
What does a big splitting energy mean?

faq.q: Is the colour always related to the energy gap?
faq.a: Yes, the colour observed is the complementary colour to the light energy absorbed by the complex ion.

faq.q: Can we predict the colour just by knowing the metal ion?
faq.a: No, we must also know the ligands present because the ligands control the magnitude of the splitting energy.

facts: The five d-orbitals are degenerate in a free metal ion.
Ligand field theory explains the splitting of these d-orbitals.
The energy difference between split levels determines the colour.
The observed colour is complementary to the colour absorbed.

quiz.say: If the energy gap ($ ext{E}{ ext{gap}}$) is small, the complex will:
quiz.show: Low $ ext{E}{ ext{gap}}$ $ ightarrow$ Visible light absorbed
quiz.why: A small energy gap means the complex absorbs lower energy light, which is towards the red end, making the observed colour complementary, like yellow.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because blue light corresponds to a larger energy gap.
wrong.1: This is wrong because all visible light energies can cause some degree of splitting.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because absorbing all visible light would result in a black colour.

quiz.say: Which factor primarily determines the magnitude of d-orbital splitting?

options.show: The oxidation state of the metal
options.say: The oxidation state of the metal

options.show: The physical state of the metal
options.say: The physical state of the metal

quiz.why: The ligands determine the strength of the interaction, which directly controls the energy difference between the split d-orbitals.

wrong.1: While important, the ligand field strength is the primary determinant of the splitting magnitude.
wrong.2: Temperature changes do not fundamentally alter the orbital splitting pattern in this context.
wrong.3: The solid or liquid state does not dictate the electronic splitting energy.

quiz.say: If a complex absorbs light at $650$ nanometres, what colour is it likely to appear?
quiz.why: Light absorbed at $650$ nanometres is in the red-orange region, so the observed colour will be the complementary colour, which is green.

wrong.0: This suggests a very large energy gap, which is not implied by the $650$ nanometre absorption.
wrong.1: This would mean it absorbs all visible wavelengths, which is not the case here.
wrong.3: This assumes the observed colour is the same as the absorbed colour.
